posts.title: What the first term asks of you
posts.excerpt: A first term at Kotoba Language is a placement, a small class, and the conversations Rotterdam already expects you to hold.
posts.content:
A first term in a new city is mostly errands that happen in a language you do not yet trust. Someone asks you to confirm a time. A school wants an answer. A landlord speaks for two minutes and waits. Kotoba Language was founded in 2016 for that stretch of ordinary speech, and for teams whose work crosses a border and still has to be understood on a Tuesday morning. The school has one address, Scheepmakerspassage 14, 3011 VH Rotterdam, Netherlands, and it teaches six languages: English, Dutch, French, German, Mandarin and Japanese.

You do not begin by picking a level from a list. You begin with an enquiry, by email at hello@kotobalanguage.example or by phone on +31 10 555 0142. The next conversation is a placement interview of 45 minutes, in person or online, and it is free. Elias Ferrand advises on placement. From what you can already say, the school writes a level and a track proposal. The level sits on the CEFR scale, from A1 to C2. The track is work, settlement or exam preparation. Registration is €45, paid once on enrolment, and then you join an intake. In 2026 those dates are 12 January, 13 April, 7 September and 9 November.

The class you join is small on purpose. The maximum is 8. Noor Abadi, director of studies, has taught English here since 2016 and treats that number as the condition for hearing everyone. There is a review at week 5. The teacher sits with the written proposal and with the weeks you have just had, and the plan moves if the group is no longer the right fit. Nothing about the term assumes the first proposal was permanent.

Most people who work in the day take the evening course: 10 weeks, two sessions of 90 minutes a week, at €590. Someone who can clear a month takes the daytime intensive, 4 weeks at 15 hours a week, for €880. A team that wants the teacher at their own workplace books a workplace group, up to 6 people, for a 10-week term at €1,980. A single hour outside the group is a private lesson at €62. Course fees may be paid in two instalments.

Settlement is the path for appointments, housing and schools. The conversation club runs one term, weekly for 90 minutes, at €150. Ana Sol Vidal teaches Dutch for new arrivals. Mariam Haddad teaches French on the settlement track. A newly arrived couple who joined the club now handle their own appointments in Dutch. That sentence is the whole aim of the club. It is a specific change in who speaks at the counter, not a general claim about fluency.

Work is the other daily use. Chidi Nwosu teaches English for work. A five-person logistics team at a shipping agency spent two 10-week terms on that track, inside the on-site group. The language in the room was the language of their handovers and their planning. Five people fit the cap of 6. The same school also prepares learners who want to sit an exam. Petra Lindgren teaches German on the exam track. The block is 8 weeks, one session of 120 minutes a week, at €470, aimed at the CEFR level named in the proposal. A customer-support team lead who moved from Beirut sat the Dutch B1 exam after three terms on the evening course. The school can say that the exam was sat. The result of any paper belongs to the candidate and to the body that marks it.

Wei-Chun Hsu teaches Mandarin, and Sanna Mäkinen teaches Japanese, on the same intakes and in the same size of class. The building does not split the calendar by language. Opening hours are Monday to Thursday, 09:00–21:00, and Friday, 09:00–17:00. Saturday, 10:00–14:00, is for placement interviews only, and Sunday is closed. If you would rather be in the room before you decide, the placement evening is the first Thursday of each month at 18:30.

Bring the meeting, the appointment or the paper you are actually facing. The first term is organised around that, in a class small enough for the teacher to hear you, with a level written down and looked at again in week 5.
